children.text: What Large Language Models Are and Why They Matter in Healthcare

A large language model is a neural network trained on vast corpora of text — books, websites, scientific literature, clinical notes, and more — to predict the most likely next token (word or word fragment) given everything that came before it. At first glance, that sounds like a narrow statistical trick. In practice, training at sufficient scale on sufficient data causes something unexpected to emerge: the model develops the ability to reason, summarize, translate, explain, and generate coherent long-form text across virtually any domain. These are not explicitly programmed capabilities. They arise from the model learning the deep structure of human knowledge as encoded in language. Healthcare is a domain that is fundamentally constituted by language: clinical notes, discharge summaries, referral letters, prior authorization requests, patient messages, diagnostic reasoning chains. That structural match is why LLMs have arrived in medicine faster, and with more initial traction, than almost any previous AI technology.

The benchmark evidence for LLM medical knowledge arrived with unusual force in 2023. Nori and colleagues at Microsoft Research published a study demonstrating that GPT-4, without any specialized medical fine-tuning or prompt engineering, exceeded the passing score on the United States Medical Licensing Examination (USMLE) by more than 20 percentage points, placing it at approximately the 90th percentile of human test-takers — a performance level that would earn a comfortable match in virtually any medical specialty. This was not a narrowly constructed benchmark; USMLE spans clinical reasoning, pharmacology, anatomy, pathophysiology, and diagnostic interpretation across all three steps of the examination sequence. GPT-4 outperformed earlier general-purpose models (GPT-3.5) and models specifically fine-tuned on medical knowledge.

Google's effort to build a domain-specialized medical LLM produced complementary evidence. Singhal and colleagues published Med-PaLM in Nature in 2023, and the follow-on Med-PaLM 2 paper in Nature Medicine (2024) demonstrated 86.5% accuracy on the USMLE-style MedQA dataset — representing more than a 19 percentage-point improvement over the original Med-PaLM and crossing the threshold of expert-level performance on medical question answering. In a pairwise evaluation of 1,066 consumer medical questions, Med-PaLM 2 answers were preferred over physician answers by a panel of physicians across eight of nine axes in their evaluation framework. These results do not mean LLMs should be making autonomous clinical decisions. But they establish definitively that general-purpose LLMs have internalized substantial medical knowledge that can be applied productively in clinical workflows — particularly in documentation, summarization, and communication tasks where the cost of a subtle factual error is mitigated by mandatory physician review.

The practical urgency is driven by a documentation crisis that predates AI. Research consistently finds that physicians spend nearly two hours on EHR tasks and administrative work for every hour of direct patient care — a ratio that reflects decades of growing regulatory requirements, billing documentation demands, and EHR complexity. In the 2024 Medscape Physician Burnout and Depression Report, 62% of physicians identified administrative tasks — charting and paperwork — as the leading contributors to burnout, with 49% of physicians overall reporting burnout symptoms. In this context, LLMs are not arriving as futuristic curiosities. They are arriving as a potential solution to a workforce crisis that is already compromising patient access and physician wellbeing at scale.

KEY DISTINCTION: LLMs deployed in clinical settings today are primarily documentation, summarization, and communication tools — not autonomous diagnostic engines. The highest-impact, most mature applications are ambient documentation (recording patient-physician conversations and generating draft clinical notes) and clinical text summarization. Diagnostic reasoning assistance is an active research frontier, not a mature deployment category, and carries meaningfully different regulatory and patient safety implications.

children.text: Ambient AI Documentation — The Highest-Value Current Use Case

If you wanted to identify the single LLM application with the largest immediate impact on physician experience and clinical workflow, the answer in 2024 and 2025 is unambiguous: ambient AI documentation. The concept is straightforward. During a clinical encounter, a microphone — room-based, worn on a badge, or embedded in a device — captures the conversation between the physician and patient. A speech-to-text engine transcribes the audio in real time. Speaker diarization algorithms separate the physician's voice from the patient's. An LLM then reads the transcript and generates a structured clinical note in the physician's preferred format — SOAP, H&P, or specialty-specific templates — populating the chief complaint, history of present illness, review of systems, physical examination, and assessment and plan. The draft note appears in the EHR after the visit. The physician reviews, edits, and signs. The encounter that once required 10 to 15 minutes of post-visit documentation now requires 1 to 3 minutes.

The commercial ecosystem for ambient AI documentation has matured rapidly. Nuance DAX Copilot — developed by Microsoft, which acquired Nuance Communications for $19.7 billion in 2022 specifically for its ambient AI documentation capabilities — has become the market leader, deployed across hundreds of health systems. A Microsoft survey of 879 clinicians in 2024 found an average of 5 minutes saved per encounter; other implementations have reported up to 50% reductions in documentation time, with some institutions reporting 7 minutes saved per visit. Nuance's own data showed a 70% reduction in feelings of burnout and fatigue among DAX users. DAX Copilot is natively integrated with Epic and other major EHRs.

Nabla, Suki AI, and Abridge are the other major ambient AI documentation platforms. Nabla has joined Epic Toolbox for Ambient Voice Recognition, enabling deployment across Epic environments in approximately 2 to 3 weeks, and has also integrated natively within Oracle Cerner — with one deployment at Aultman Health System reporting clinicians saving 30 to 60 minutes per day on documentation. Abridge, a Carnegie Mellon spinout backed by UPMC, powers the largest prospective clinical study of ambient AI to date. The competition among these platforms is fierce, which is favorable for health systems: integration depth, specialty-specific template libraries, multilingual support, and billing code suggestion capabilities are differentiating rapidly.

The most rigorous evidence for ambient AI documentation's clinical impact comes from a study published in JAMA Network Open in 2024. The study evaluated the Abridge ambient AI scribe across 186 clinicians at six US health systems over a 30-day intervention period. Physicians using the ambient AI scribe experienced a net reduction of 13.9 percentage points in burnout and 6.2 percentage points in severe burnout. Critically, the study measured objective outcomes — not just satisfaction surveys — including significant reductions in after-hours documentation time, the so-called "pajama time" that has been a defining feature of modern physician dissatisfaction. A companion study (AJMC, 2024) corroborated these findings with objective EHR usage data, showing reduced time spent in the EHR after business hours.

MUSC Health reported a 20% reduction in documentation time following DAX Copilot adoption.

The market is now highly competitive, with Epic's own ambient AI tools, Nabla, Abridge, and Suki all offering EHR-integrated solutions — driving feature velocity and downward pricing pressure that benefits health systems evaluating deployment.

steps.description: A speech-to-text engine converts the audio to a text transcript. Speaker diarization algorithms identify and separate the physician's voice from the patient's, preserving the conversational structure needed for clinical note generation. Modern systems achieve low word error rates even with medical terminology, accents, and background noise.
steps.title: Real-Time Transcription

steps.description: The LLM reads the full transcript and generates a structured clinical note in the physician's preferred format: chief complaint, HPI, ROS, physical examination findings, assessment, and plan. Specialty-specific templates (cardiology H&P, psychiatry intake, orthopedic follow-up) ensure the output matches clinical workflow expectations.
steps.title: Clinical Note Generation

steps.description: The draft note appears in the EHR immediately after — or in some systems, during — the visit. The physician reviews, edits for accuracy and completeness, adds clinical judgment that was not verbalized, and signs. This step typically takes 1 to 3 minutes versus 10 to 15 minutes writing from scratch. No AI-generated content enters the permanent record without physician attestation.
steps.title: Physician Review

steps.description: Advanced ambient AI systems analyze the note content and suggest appropriate E&M (Evaluation and Management) billing codes based on the documented complexity of medical decision-making. The physician confirms. This reduces the under-coding that costs practices significant revenue annually and eliminates the manual code-selection step from the post-visit workflow.
steps.title: Billing Code Suggestion

steps.description: Some systems apply automated checks to the generated note, flagging potentially missing elements — no follow-up plan documented, no medication reconciliation completed, drug interaction mentioned during the visit that was not addressed in the assessment and plan. These flags are advisory, not blocking, and the physician makes all final clinical decisions.

children.text: Clinical Summarization and Communication — Expanding the Use Cases

Ambient documentation captures real-time conversations and structures them into clinical notes. But the LLM use case landscape in clinical settings extends considerably beyond the encounter itself. A substantial fraction of physician administrative burden consists of reading, synthesizing, and writing documents that are not generated in real time — discharge summaries, referral letters, prior authorization justification letters, responses to patient portal messages, and comprehensive summaries of complex patient histories. LLMs trained on clinical text can meaningfully assist with all of these tasks, always with a physician review step before any output enters the permanent record or reaches another party.

Discharge summary generation is one of the most consequential secondary use cases. The discharge summary is a medically and legally critical document that must accurately capture the entire inpatient encounter: presenting diagnoses, hospital course, procedures performed, medications prescribed, follow-up instructions, and pending results. Writing a thorough discharge summary for a complex patient — one with multiple active problems, a lengthy hospitalization, and several specialist consultations — can take 30 to 60 minutes of physician time. Delays in discharge summary completion have been documented as a source of care coordination failures when patients transition to post-acute settings. An LLM that reads the entire inpatient record — nursing notes, lab results, procedure reports, specialist notes — and drafts a structured discharge summary reduces this bottleneck substantially, even when the physician edits the draft significantly before signing.

Prior authorization represents one of the most reviled administrative burdens in US medicine. Physicians and their staff spend hours per week drafting clinical justification letters for payers — compiling relevant history, citing treatment guidelines, documenting prior treatment failures, and formatting submissions to insurer-specific requirements. LLMs can draft these letters by reading the relevant EHR data for a specific patient and the clinical indication, producing a first draft that the physician or care coordinator reviews, edits, and submits. The time savings per authorization request are meaningful; when multiplied across the thousands of prior authorizations processed annually by a busy health system, the aggregate administrative burden reduction is substantial.

Patient portal message management has quietly become a significant physician time burden. Epic's MyChart messaging volume surged dramatically following the COVID-19 pandemic as patients became accustomed to communicating with care teams digitally. Epic integrated LLM-drafted response suggestions into MyChart's provider inbox — presenting physicians with a draft response to each patient message that the physician can accept, edit, or discard entirely before sending. This model keeps the physician in complete control of the communication while reducing the effort required from writing to reviewing — a task that takes seconds rather than minutes when the AI's draft is largely correct. The same "draft then review" pattern applies to referral letters: the LLM synthesizes the relevant clinical history for the specialist from the EHR, the physician edits and sends.

Medical record summarization for complex patients deserves particular attention. A patient with decades of chronic illness — heart failure, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, multiple prior hospitalizations — may have an EHR containing thousands of pages of records. When a new specialist sees this patient for the first time, or when the patient presents to an emergency department at an unfamiliar institution, the clinician faces an impossible reading task. An LLM that reads the entire record and generates a structured summary — problem list, medication history with rationale, relevant procedures, allergies, pertinent social history — transforms the information access problem from one of incompleteness to one of synthesis. The physician still reads critically and supplements the summary with direct inquiry, but the cognitive load of navigating a massive unstructured record is dramatically reduced.

body.analogy: An LLM drafting a discharge summary from an inpatient record is like a skilled research assistant who has read every chart note, lab result, and consultant report — and prepares a structured briefing for the attending to review, edit, and sign. The attending's clinical judgment and accountability remain unchanged; what changes is how much of the reading and initial drafting work the assistant handles versus the physician doing it alone at 9pm.
body.concept: Why LLM summarization reduces burden without reducing physician accountability

children.text: The Hallucination Problem and Clinical Risk

Every clinician, health administrator, and AI procurement officer evaluating LLM tools for clinical use must understand one fundamental characteristic of the technology: LLMs hallucinate. Hallucination is the tendency of LLMs to generate text that is fluent, confident, and plausible-sounding but factually incorrect. It is not primarily a calibration failure — a matter of the model expressing certainty when it should express uncertainty. It is an emergent property of the architecture: models are trained to generate the most statistically likely next token, and sometimes the most statistically likely continuation of a clinical statement is factually wrong. The model has no ground-truth knowledge to check against; it has only learned patterns in text. When those patterns lead it astray, it proceeds confidently down the wrong path.

In clinical contexts, hallucination takes forms that range from mildly inconvenient to genuinely dangerous. An LLM summarizing a complex patient record might fabricate a lab value that was never ordered, misattribute a medication to the wrong encounter, invent a procedure that does not appear in the record, or generate an incorrect allergy entry. A study published in npj Digital Medicine (2025) that evaluated LLMs across 18 experimental configurations and 12,999 clinician-annotated sentences found a 1.47% hallucination rate and a 3.45% omission rate in clinical note generation tasks. A separate evaluation of LLMs for emergency department encounter summaries found that 42% of GPT-4 generated summaries contained hallucinations and 47% omitted clinically relevant information, though only 10% had inaccuracies in any individual data element. Rates vary substantially by task, model, and clinical domain — but the risk is present across all configurations studied.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation, or RAG, is the primary technical mitigation for hallucination in clinical summarization tasks. In a RAG architecture, the LLM is not generating from its parametric memory — the patterns learned during training — but is instead grounded in specific source documents retrieved for that query. For clinical summarization, this means the LLM generates the discharge summary by reading the actual EHR data for that patient, with those documents explicitly provided in the context window. Any statement it generates can, in principle, be traced back to a specific source document. RAG substantially reduces hallucination rates compared to pure generation from parametric memory, and it enables automated citation — each sentence in the generated summary can be linked to the source note or lab result it was derived from. But RAG does not eliminate hallucination entirely. Models can still misread, misattribute, or incorrectly synthesize information even when the source documents are present in the context.

The critical operational implication of hallucination is not that LLMs cannot be used clinically — the evidence suggests they can reduce burden substantially when deployed appropriately. The implication is that the "human in the loop" requirement is non-negotiable, and it must be enforced structurally, not merely requested by policy. EHR workflow integrations should be designed so that AI-generated text cannot enter the permanent medical record — a signed clinical note, a sent patient message, a submitted prior authorization letter — without explicit physician attestation that the content has been reviewed and is accurate. Workflows that make it easy to approve AI drafts with minimal review, or that present AI output in ways that encourage passive acceptance rather than active reading, create structural conditions for hallucination-driven errors.

body.message: No LLM-generated clinical content should enter the medical record or be communicated to a patient without explicit physician review and attestation. Studies consistently find factual errors — fabricated lab values, incorrect medication attributions, omitted clinically relevant information — in LLM-generated clinical summaries, even when the text reads fluently and confidently. Treating AI-drafted clinical notes as final documents without thorough review is a patient safety risk. Workflow design should enforce active physician attestation, not merely permit it.
body.title: LLMs Hallucinate — Always Require Human Review

children.text: Regulatory, Privacy, and Governance Considerations

The deployment of LLMs in clinical settings intersects with three distinct regulatory domains: HIPAA privacy and security, FDA device regulation, and institutional governance. Each creates obligations that health system leaders, clinical informatics professionals, and procurement teams must navigate before deployment. Understanding these frameworks is not a legal formality — it is the infrastructure that determines whether a health system's LLM deployment is safe, legally defensible, and sustainable.

HIPAA's Business Associate Agreement requirement is the first and most immediate compliance consideration. Any cloud service that stores or processes Protected Health Information (PHI) on behalf of a covered entity must sign a BAA, which obligates them to safeguard that information under HIPAA's privacy and security rules — including breach notification, minimum necessary use, and appropriate technical safeguards. This requirement applies to LLMs processing clinical data: the vendor providing the LLM service must be willing and able to sign a BAA. Microsoft's Azure OpenAI Service (which provides GPT-4 class models) is HIPAA-eligible under Microsoft's enterprise BAA, making it a viable platform for health systems building clinical AI tools. Google Cloud's Vertex AI is similarly HIPAA-eligible under Google's BAA. Amazon Bedrock provides access to Claude, Llama, and other models in a HIPAA-eligible environment. The critical negative case: the public consumer version of ChatGPT at chatgpt.com operates under general terms of service and is not covered by a BAA. Entering any patient information into the public ChatGPT interface constitutes a reportable HIPAA breach.

FDA regulatory classification for LLM-based clinical tools depends on function. The 21st Century Cures Act created a carve-out from FDA device regulation for certain Clinical Decision Support (CDS) software — specifically, software that displays or analyzes patient-specific information to support a clinical decision, when a clinician can independently review the basis for the recommendation. Documentation tools (ambient AI scribes), summarization tools (discharge summary drafters), and communication tools (patient message drafting) generally qualify for this CDS exemption because the physician reviews the AI output and applies independent clinical judgment. In January 2025, the FDA issued draft guidance titled "Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions: Lifecycle Management and Marketing Submission Recommendations," signaling increasing regulatory attention to AI in clinical workflows. LLM-based tools that make autonomous treatment recommendations — generating medication orders, specifying doses, issuing diagnoses without mandatory physician review — are Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) subject to FDA premarket review. As of 2025, the FDA had authorized over 1,250 AI-enabled medical devices, with the agency actively developing a framework for the total product lifecycle regulation of adaptive AI systems.

Algorithmic bias is a governance consideration that deserves explicit attention. LLMs trained predominantly on medical literature and clinical notes that underrepresent certain populations — racial and ethnic minorities, patients with limited English proficiency, patients with rare diseases — may generate clinical content that reflects or amplifies existing disparities. A discharge summary generator trained primarily on notes written for English-speaking, well-insured patients at academic medical centers may perform differently when deployed at safety-net hospitals serving predominantly non-English-speaking populations. Health systems deploying clinical LLMs should require demographic subgroup performance data from vendors and should monitor for differential performance post-deployment.

The highest-risk clinical LLM use cases are those where the LLM output directly drives a clinical decision without meaningful physician review — diagnostic suggestions accepted without verification, medication orders generated from AI drafts, patient triage decisions made by autonomous chatbots. The lowest-risk use cases are administrative: documentation drafting, summarization, communication drafting — where a physician always reviews before the output enters the record or reaches another party. Governance frameworks should map every LLM use case against this risk spectrum before deployment authorization.

children.text: Clinical AI governance is the organizational infrastructure that makes LLM deployment safe over time. Health systems deploying clinical LLMs should establish: a clinical AI governance committee with representation from clinical leadership, informatics, legal, compliance, and patient advocacy; a pre-deployment validation process that tests AI performance on the institution's own patient population before enterprise rollout; ongoing post-deployment monitoring for accuracy degradation, bias, and unexpected usage patterns; structured clinician training on the limitations of LLMs (particularly hallucination risk) so that physician review is genuinely critical rather than perfunctory; and a clear incident reporting and escalation pathway for AI errors — so that when hallucination-driven errors occur (and they will), the organization can learn and respond systematically rather than treating each incident as an isolated anomaly.

points: Large language models like GPT-4 have demonstrated expert-level performance on medical knowledge benchmarks — GPT-4 at approximately the 90th percentile on USMLE (Nori et al., Microsoft 2023) and Med-PaLM 2 at 86.5% accuracy on MedQA (Nature Medicine, 2024) — but their primary clinical deployment is not autonomous diagnosis. It is documentation, summarization, and communication assistance, where a physician always reviews before the output enters the record.

Ambient AI documentation — recording patient-physician conversations and generating draft clinical notes — is the highest-value, most mature LLM clinical use case. A JAMA Network Open 2024 study of 186 clinicians across 6 health systems found a net 13.9 percentage-point reduction in burnout after one month of using the Abridge ambient AI scribe, with significant reductions in after-hours documentation time.

LLMs hallucinate: they generate plausible-sounding but factually incorrect text confidently, and this is an architectural characteristic, not a fixable bug. Studies find hallucination rates from 1.47% in structured clinical note generation to 42% of summaries containing at least one error in ED encounter summarization — making human review of all AI-generated clinical content a non-negotiable patient safety requirement.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), where the LLM is grounded in specific source documents (the actual EHR record), substantially reduces but does not eliminate hallucination in clinical summarization. RAG also enables automated citation — each generated sentence can be traced to a source document — which is becoming a standard requirement for trustworthy clinical AI tools.

HIPAA compliance requires a Business Associate Agreement with any LLM vendor processing Protected Health Information. Microsoft Azure OpenAI, Google Vertex AI, and Amazon Bedrock are HIPAA-eligible under enterprise BAAs. The public consumer versions of ChatGPT, Claude.ai, and Gemini are not covered by BAAs, and entering patient data into these tools constitutes a reportable HIPAA breach.

FDA regulatory classification depends on function: ambient documentation tools and summarization tools may qualify for Clinical Decision Support exemptions under the 21st Century Cures Act; LLM tools that make autonomous treatment recommendations are Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) subject to FDA premarket review. The FDA's January 2025 draft guidance on AI-enabled device software signals increasing regulatory rigor for clinical AI across the product lifecycle.

Clinical AI governance — a committee with cross-functional representation, pre-deployment validation on the institution's own patient population, ongoing monitoring for accuracy and bias, structured clinician training on hallucination risk, and a formal incident reporting pathway — is the organizational infrastructure that determines whether LLM deployment is safe and sustainable. Technology without governance is a patient safety liability.

body.explanation: HIPAA requires that any vendor who handles Protected Health Information on behalf of a covered entity sign a Business Associate Agreement (BAA), which obligates the vendor to safeguard that information under HIPAA's privacy and security rules. Consumer AI tools — the public versions of ChatGPT, Claude.ai, and Gemini — operate under general terms of service, not a BAA. Entering patient name, diagnosis, and clinical history into these tools constitutes a HIPAA breach that must be reported to HHS OCR. HIPAA-compliant LLM access is available through enterprise agreements: Microsoft Azure OpenAI, Google Vertex AI, and Amazon Bedrock all offer HIPAA-eligible environments with signed BAAs. Option A is incorrect — the concern is legal, not capability. Option C is false — AI assistance with documentation is legally permitted when the tool operates under a BAA. Option D is incorrect — ambient documentation and referral letter drafting tools are typically covered by the CDS software exemptions in the 21st Century Cures Act, not requiring FDA premarket clearance, provided a physician reviews and attests the output.
